title: Degree and Radian Measure
learningObjective: Convert between degrees and radians. Draw angles in standard position.

faqs.question: What is an angle, and what are the initial side, terminal side, and vertex?
faqs.answer:
An angle is formed by two rays joined at a shared starting point, called the vertex. In trigonometry, we think of an angle as a rotation: the initial side is where the angle starts (before any rotation), and the terminal side is where the angle ends up after rotating.

The angle is the rotation from the initial side to the terminal side, pivoting at the vertex.

faqs.question: What does it mean for an angle to be in standard position?
faqs.answer:
An angle is in standard position when its vertex sits at the origin and its initial side lies exactly along the positive x-axis. This gives every angle a consistent, predictable starting point, which is essential once you start comparing angles or plotting them on the coordinate plane.

Standard position: vertex at the origin, initial side along the positive x-axis.

faqs.question: Why do some angles have a positive measure and others a negative measure?
faqs.answer:
The sign of an angle tells you which direction it was rotated. An angle measured counterclockwise from the initial side is positive; an angle measured clockwise is negative. For example, +60° and −60° are the same amount of rotation in opposite directions; the sign just records which way you turned. Beyond TR1: CheckIt's TR1 angles are all positive, between 0° and 360°, so you will not see negative angles on this check. Later on, keep in mind that the terminal side alone doesn't show the direction or the number of turns: 300° and −60° end on the same side, and only the turn arc tells them apart.

Counterclockwise (teal, labeled +60°, turning up) is positive; clockwise (orange, labeled −60°, turning down) is negative — same size angle, opposite direction.

faqs.question: What is a radian, and how is it actually defined?
faqs.answer:
One radian is the measure of a central angle that cuts out an arc exactly as long as the circle's radius. Picture taking the radius of a circle, bending it around the edge of the circle like a piece of string, and marking where it ends — the angle formed at the center is exactly 1 radian.

When the arc (orange) is exactly as long as the radius, the angle it creates is defined as 1 radian — about 57.3°.

faqs.question: Why are there 2π radians in a full circle?
faqs.answer: This comes straight from the circumference formula. The circumference of a circle is C = 2πr — in other words, the full distance around the circle is always 2π times the radius. Since one radian is defined as the angle created by an arc equal to one radius (faq-4), and the whole circle's arc length is 2π radii, a full circle must measure exactly 2π radians.

faqs.question: How do I convert an angle from degrees to radians?
faqs.answer:
Multiply the degree measure by π/180°. This works because 180° and π radians represent the exact same amount of rotation (half a circle), so π/180° is just a conversion factor equal to 1.
Worked Example

Convert \( 60° \) to radians:

\( 60° \times \dfrac{\pi}{180°} = \dfrac{60\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \)

faqs.question: How do I convert an angle from radians to degrees?
faqs.answer:
Multiply the radian measure by 180°/π — the same conversion factor from faq-6, just flipped upside down since you're converting in the opposite direction.
Worked Example

Convert \( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) to degrees:

\( \dfrac{\pi}{6} \times \dfrac{180°}{\pi} = \dfrac{180°}{6} = 30° \)

faqs.question: How do I sketch an angle in standard position if I'm given its measure in degrees?
faqs.answer:
Start by drawing the initial side along the positive x-axis. Then estimate what fraction of a full circle (360°) the angle represents, and rotate the terminal side that fraction of the way around — counterclockwise if positive, clockwise if negative. You don't need to be perfectly precise, but CheckIt's TR1 angles are multiples of 30° and 45°, so aim for the right 30° or 45° mark, not just the right quadrant: 300° and 330° are both in Quadrant IV but are different drawings.
Worked Example

Sketch \( 120° \): since \( 120° \) is a bit more than a quarter turn (90°) but less than a half turn (180°), rotate the terminal side counterclockwise into Quadrant II, 30° past the positive y-axis, so closer to the positive y-axis than to the negative x-axis.

faqs.question: How do I sketch an angle in standard position if I'm given its measure in radians?
faqs.answer: Convert the radian measure to degrees first (faq-7) if that helps you visualize it, or use benchmark radian angles you're building familiarity with: π/2 is a quarter turn, π is a half turn, 3π/2 is three-quarters of a turn, and 2π is a full circle. Then estimate where your angle falls relative to those benchmarks.

faqs.question: How do I know which direction to draw an angle — clockwise or counterclockwise?
faqs.answer: Check the sign. A positive angle measure always means counterclockwise rotation from the initial side; a negative angle measure always means clockwise rotation. If no sign is written, assume positive (counterclockwise). Beyond TR1: CheckIt's TR1 angles are all positive, between 0° and 360°, so you will not see negative angles on this check.

faqs.question: Why do radian measures often involve π, and what does a value like 7π/6 actually mean?
faqs.answer: Since a full turn is exactly 2π radians, familiar angles have measures that are convenient fractions of π, so we keep π in the expression rather than converting to a decimal. In 7π/6, each slice measures π/6, or 30°. Six slices make a half turn (π), and twelve make a full turn (2π). Seven slices give 210°, which puts the terminal side 30° past the negative x-axis, in Quadrant III. Reading the denominator as "the size of each slice" and the numerator as "how many slices you rotated through" makes these values much easier to picture. (Radian measures don't have to contain π; 1 or 2 radians are angles too. CheckIt's TR1 angles are multiples of π.)

faqs.question: How does everything in TR1 set up the rest of the trig unit?
faqs.answer: Standard position and the degree/radian relationship are the language every later trig topic is written in. TR2's coterminal angles only make sense once you understand rotation and standard position. TR3's right-triangle trig and TR5's unit circle both rely on angles being placed and measured consistently. Radians specifically become essential once you reach calculus, where nearly all trig work is done exclusively in radians.

faqs.question: Why do radians matter beyond just being another unit for angles?
faqs.answer: Radians aren't just a different way to write the same angle — they connect an angle directly to actual distance along a circle, since the radian definition is built from arc length and radius. This connection becomes essential in later math and physics: arc length, angular velocity, and eventually calculus with trig functions all rely on radians specifically, because degrees don't have that same built-in relationship to distance.

guided.title: Understand the Radian Definition
guided.prompt: I'm learning what a radian is. Don't define a radian for me. Ask me questions until I can explain why wrapping one radius around the circle gives 1 radian, and why a half turn is π. Then write a short explanation with one subtle error, and I'll find it.

guided.title: Practice Degree-Radian Conversion

Convert five CheckIt-style angles (special angles between 0° and 360°, some in degrees and some in radians) and get two wrong in realistic ways (dividing by 360, using the wrong factor, leaving π in a degree answer). I'll grade your work and explain each fix.

guided.title: Build Intuition for Radian Benchmarks
guided.prompt: I'm trying to build a mental picture of common radian angles like π/2, π, 3π/2, and 2π. Can you help me visualize each one as a fraction of a full turn around a circle? Then give me a radian value like 7π/6 or 5π/4 and help me figure out roughly where it lands without converting to degrees first. Then tell me where 11π/6 and 2π/3 land, getting one wrong, and ask me which one you got wrong and how I know.

guided.title: Beyond TR1: Connect Radians to Arc Length
guided.prompt: Beyond TR1: I've learned that a radian is defined using arc length and radius. Before you explain anything, ask me to predict how far a wheel with a 1-foot radius rolls in a half turn. Then help me check my prediction, and point out where my reasoning was right.

paths.label: TR1: Degree and Radian Measure
paths.intro: Builds to the TR1 check: drawing angles in standard position and converting between degrees and radians.

stages.desc: Two quick skills TR1 leans on. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Simplify fractions over 180
stops.target: Reduce fractions like \(\dfrac{150}{180}\) to lowest terms by dividing by common factors.
stops.solution: 120/180: both divide by 60, giving 2/3. 300/180: both divide by 60, giving 5/3. If you do not see the biggest factor, divide by any common factor first (10, 5, 9 or 15 often work), then keep going.
stops.reflect: What is a quick first step when you do not see the biggest common factor?

stops.title: Standard position and quadrants
stops.target: An angle in standard position starts on the positive \(x\)-axis (initial side) and rotates counterclockwise for positive angles. Know which quadrant each range of angles ends in.
stops.cold: In which quadrant (or on which axis) does each angle end? \(120^\circ\), \(300^\circ\), \(210^\circ\)
stops.coldPlain: In which quadrant (or on which axis) does each angle end: 120 degrees, 300 degrees, 210 degrees?
stops.coldA: \(120^\circ\): Quadrant II. \(300^\circ\): Quadrant IV. \(210^\circ\): Quadrant III.
stops.solution: Quadrant I is strictly between 0 and 90 degrees (0 < θ < 90), II is 90 < θ < 180, III is 180 < θ < 270, and IV is 270 < θ < 360. Angles of 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees land on an axis, not in a quadrant. So 120 is in II, 300 in IV, and 210 in III.
stops.mistake: Counting quadrants clockwise, or starting from the y-axis.
stops.againA: \(60^\circ\): Quadrant I. \(270^\circ\): on the negative \(y\)-axis (not in a quadrant). \(170^\circ\): Quadrant II.
stops.reflect: Which four angles from 0° up to (but not including) 360° have terminal sides on the coordinate axes?

stages.desc: One stop per skill on the TR1 check: drawing angles and converting both ways.

stops.title: Draw a degree angle
stops.target: Draw an angle in degrees in standard position: find the nearest axis, then go the extra amount past it, counterclockwise.
stops.note: I drew the angle on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: where the initial side is, which direction I rotated, which quadrant or axis the terminal side ends in, and how far past the nearest axis it is. Check my drawing.
stops.coldA: Go past \(90^\circ\) by another \(30^\circ\), into Quadrant II, closer to the positive \(y\)-axis.[[graph:d120]]
stops.solution: Start on the positive x-axis and rotate counterclockwise. 120 = 90 + 30, so pass the positive y-axis and go 30 degrees more: one third of the way from the positive y-axis to the negative x-axis, in Quadrant II. Draw an arc with an arrow to show the direction.
stops.mistake: Rotating clockwise, or forgetting the arc that shows the rotation. (CheckIt's own answer picture shows a small arc without an arrowhead; drawing the arrow is still good practice.)
stops.againA: \(300^\circ = 360^\circ - 60^\circ\): stop \(60^\circ\) short of a full turn, in Quadrant IV.[[graph:d300]]
stops.stretchA: \(180^\circ + 30^\circ\): just past the negative \(x\)-axis, in Quadrant III.[[graph:d210]]
stops.reflect: How do benchmarks like \(90^\circ\), \(180^\circ\), and \(270^\circ\) help you draw quickly?

stops.title: Degrees to radians
stops.target: Convert degrees to radians by multiplying by \(\dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ}\) and simplifying. (\(180^\circ = \pi\) radians.)
stops.solution: Multiply by pi/180: 135 * pi/180 = 135pi/180. Simplify 135/180 = 3/4 (divide by 45). Answer: 3pi/4.
stops.mistake: Multiplying by 180/pi (the wrong direction), which leaves degrees and pi in a strange mix.
stops.reflect: How do you remember which fraction to multiply by?

stops.title: Radians to degrees
stops.target: Convert radians to degrees by multiplying by \(\dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}\). For the multiples of \(\pi\) used here, the \(\pi\) factors cancel.
stops.solution: Multiply by 180/pi. The pi cancels: (4/3)(180) = 240 degrees. Shortcut: replace pi with 180 degrees, so 4(180)/3 = 240.
stops.mistake: Keeping the pi in the answer.

stops.title: Draw a radian angle
stops.target: Draw an angle in radians by thinking in slices of a half turn (\(\pi\)): \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) is 11 slices of \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), one slice short of a full turn (\(2\pi\)).
stops.note: I drew the angle on paper. I'll either upload a photo or describe it: where the initial side is, which direction I rotated, which quadrant or axis the terminal side ends in, and how far past the nearest axis it is. Check my drawing.
stops.coldA: \(\pi\) is a half turn cut into 6 slices, so a full turn \(2\pi\) is 12 slices; go 11 of them. That is \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) short of the positive \(x\)-axis, in Quadrant IV.[[graph:r330]]
stops.solution: Each slice is pi/6, or 30 degrees. pi is 6 slices (a half turn) and 2pi is 12 slices (a full turn). 11pi/6 is 11 slices: one slice short of a full turn, just below the positive x-axis, in Quadrant IV. If it helps, convert: 11pi/6 = 330 degrees.
stops.mistake: Cutting the whole circle into 6 slices instead of the half turn, which makes 11pi/6 look like almost two full turns.
stops.againA: \(\dfrac{4\pi}{3} = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\): Quadrant III.[[graph:r240]]\(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): halfway to the positive \(y\)-axis, Quadrant I.[[graph:r45]]
stops.reflect: How can comparing a radian angle to \(\pi\) and \(2\pi\) tell you where it lands?
stops.stretch: Draw \(\pi\) and \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\). Which quadrant is each in?
stops.stretchA: \(\pi\) is a half turn, ending on the negative \(x\)-axis.[[graph:r180]]\(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) is three quarter turns, ending on the negative \(y\)-axis.[[graph:r270]]Neither is in a quadrant: an angle whose terminal side is on an axis is not in any quadrant.

stages.desc: A practice check in the same two-part format as the TR1 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Draw a degree angle and a radian angle in standard position, and convert each to the other unit.
stops.cold:
(a) Draw \(120^\circ\) in standard position. Convert it to radians.
(b) Draw \(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\) in standard position. Convert it to degrees.
stops.coldPlain: (a) Draw 120 degrees in standard position and convert it to radians. (b) Draw 4pi/3 in standard position and convert it to degrees.
stops.note: I drew both angles on paper. I'll upload a photo, or for each one I'll tell you where it starts, which way I turned, where it ends, and how far past the nearest axis. Check both.
stops.solution: (a) 120 = 90 + 30: 30 degrees past the positive y-axis, in Quadrant II. 120 * pi/180 = 2pi/3. (b) 4pi/3 is pi/3, or 60 degrees, past a half turn (pi), in Quadrant III. 4pi/3 * 180/pi = 240 degrees.
stops.mistake: Drawing clockwise, or converting in the wrong direction.
stops.again:
(a) Draw \(60^\circ\) and convert it to radians.
(b) Draw \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) and convert it to degrees.
stops.againA: (a) Two thirds of the way to the positive \(y\)-axis, Quadrant I. \(60^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).[[graph:d60]](b) \(2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\), Quadrant IV. \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6} = 330^\circ\).[[graph:r330]]
stops.reflect: Which is easier for you to picture, degrees or radians? What will help with the other?
stops.stretch: Beyond TR1 (CheckIt's TR1 angles are positive, but negative angles come up later): (a) Draw \(-120^\circ\) and convert it to radians. (b) Draw \(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) and convert it to degrees.
stops.stretchA: (a) Rotate \(120^\circ\) clockwise: \(30^\circ\) past the negative \(y\)-axis, in Quadrant III. \(-120^\circ = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).[[graph:dn120]](b) Rotate \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) (\(135^\circ\)) clockwise: \(45^\circ\) past the negative \(y\)-axis, in Quadrant III. \(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4} = -135^\circ\).[[graph:rn135]]Notice that \(-120^\circ\) ends on the same side as \(240^\circ\). Only the direction of the turn arc tells them apart.
